items.title: Profitable businesses fail when cash runs out
items.claim: A construction firm books £5 million revenue and £500,000 profit in 2023 but customers pay 120 days after invoicing while suppliers demand 30 days. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: Strong cash position because of the reported profit
A cash flow gap large enough to threaten survival, despite profitability — overtrading
Profit and cash will be identical
Suppliers must accept 120-day payment by law

items.reveal:
Carillion, the UK construction giant, reported £147 million profit in 2016 and collapsed in January 2018 with £1.5 billion of debt. A large part of the gap between profit and cash came from long receivable cycles on government contracts combined with aggressive revenue recognition.

'Profit is opinion; cash is fact' is an accounting saying with an empirical basis. The UK Insolvency Service reports that 80%+ of business failures involve a cash-flow rather than profitability problem.
items.why: Reported profit can lead, lag or diverge from cash entirely. Working capital management is often what separates surviving and failing firms.

items.title: CSR and financial performance — the evidence is mixed but tilts positive
items.claim: Friede, Busch and Bassen's 2015 meta-analysis aggregated over 2,000 studies on the link between ESG (environmental, social, governance) factors and corporate financial performance. What did it find?

options.text: ESG and financial performance are negatively related across the board
Around 90% of studies found a non-negative relationship; the majority showed positive correlation between ESG performance and financial performance, though magnitudes are modest
No study has examined this question
ESG is required to be at least cost-neutral by law

items.reveal:
Friede, Busch and Bassen (Journal of Sustainable Finance and Investment, 2015) reviewed 2,200 empirical studies dating back to the 1970s. About 90% reported non-negative ESG-CFP relationships; ~63% reported positive.

Milton Friedman's 1970 New York Times Magazine essay ('The Social Responsibility of Business is to Increase its Profits') argued the opposite. The empirical question turns out to be less stark than either side claims — the effect is usually positive but small, and depends on which ESG element and which industry.
items.why: Strategy debates about CSR are often conducted without reference to the evidence. The aggregate finding is messier than either 'CSR is profitable' or 'CSR is a cost' implies.

items.title: UK Supreme Court ruled Uber drivers were workers, not self-employed
items.claim: In February 2021, the UK Supreme Court ruled on the employment status of Uber drivers. What did it decide?

options.text: Drivers were correctly classified as self-employed
Drivers were 'workers' under UK law, entitled to minimum wage, paid holiday and pension auto-enrolment
Drivers were 'employees' with full unfair-dismissal rights
Uber was banned from operating in the UK

items.reveal:
The case ran from a 2016 Employment Tribunal decision to the Supreme Court. Lord Leggatt's judgment held that Uber's contract terms could not displace the reality of control: Uber set fares, terms, the rating system and routes.

Uber subsequently announced UK drivers would be paid minimum wage and pension contributions. The judgment did not give drivers full 'employee' status (no protection against unfair dismissal). Similar litigation has run in California, France and the Netherlands.
items.why: UK employment law has three statuses (employee, worker, self-employed). The 'worker' middle category was created in 1996; gig economy litigation has been the main test of where the line falls.
